newsitem.title: UK: UK SFA toughens rules for executive responsibility.
newsitem.headline: UK SFA toughens rules for executive responsibility.

text.p: British financial markets regulator the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) on Tuesday published proposals aimed at making easier the identification of those responsible when a company suffers catastrophic failure.

Under the new proposals, the burden of proof falls on senior management rather than the regulator. The present regulations, although assigning ultimate responsibility to top executives, are thought too vague to be sufficiently effective.
The new rules have been drawn up since the former chairman of Barings, Peter Baring, and his deputy Andrew Tuckey, escaped prosecution under SFA rules.
"Barings had a matrix management and internal control structure which is typical of internationally active investment firms," said the SFA in a statement.
"The difference with Barings is that the structure ultimately did not work."

The new proposals include making "the senior nominated officer in each firm directly responsible and accountable for ensuring that not only are the control structures in place in the firm but that they are working effectively."
SFA chairman Nicholas Durlacher moved to justify the new rules, which are thought likely to stir up controversy.
"We are not proposing that senior executives take responsibility for all the actions of their employees," said Durlacher.

"However, we do think that SFA should have the right to require senior executives formally to justify their conduct and competence in the event of a management failure which is so serious that it threatens the future of the firm."
A consultation period is due to end on October 21.
The SFA is the regulatory organisation responsible for regulating members of all the organised city investment markets, with about 1,350 firms and 40,000 individuals regulated by it.
